name: Vello CPU (sparse strips renderer)
baseline: Skia (CPU pipeline) and Cairo; also Rust tiny-skia, raqote, AGG, JUCE
workload: Time for 1000 render calls of a single shape (rectangles, many-segment polygons, curves, strokes; solid/gradient/image paints) at sizes 8x8 to 256x256 on a 512x600 pixmap, single-threaded and 8-thread, in a fork of the Blend2D benchmark harness.
claimed_speedup: Thesis: Vello CPU 'outperforms nearly all other renderers, including Skia or Cairo, as the shape size increases'; Blend2D still wins in the vast majority of cases. Fill-Solid-RectU 256x256 single-threaded: Vello CPU 14.2 ms vs Skia 50.3 ms (about 3.5x faster, derived from page data) and Cairo 21.9 ms (about 1.5x faster, derived from page data) per 1000 renders; Blend2D 10.8 ms. At small sizes (8x8, 16x16) Skia, AGG and JUCE are faster in some tests. Multi-threaded 8T mode adds speedups up to about 4x on large shapes.
compiler_and_flags: Rust crates built with target-feature=+avx2 on x86 (no extra flags on ARM); build flags of the C++ baselines (Skia, Cairo, Blend2D) not stated in the thesis
hardware: Apple M1 Pro (8 cores, 16 GB) thesis results; Intel Core i9-14900K also run, per vello_chart manifest.json
tradeoffs: Rust crate (vello_cpu); C bindings exist in a separate repo (LaurenzV/vello_cpu_c) so C++ use needs FFI. Weak for very small shapes because of the fixed 4x4 tile size. Supports multi-threading and NEON/AVX2 SIMD.
caveats: Evidence is an ETH Zurich master's thesis (PDF checked into LaurenzV/master-thesis, read via raw.githubusercontent.com) by the Vello CPU author, so the benchmark is first-party for Vello CPU even though the harness is a fork of Blend2D's. Blend2D is faster in nearly all tests, so this is not a win over the category's best. Thesis reports M1 Pro only; interactive results for M1 Pro and i9-14900K live at laurenzv.github.io/vello_chart (blocked here, not opened; repo manifest.json read). The Vello repo README itself has no numbers. Thesis is not formally peer reviewed beyond the university examination, hence B.
found_via: WebSearch: 'sparse strips CPU GPU 2D vector graphics rendering Vello thesis benchmark Skia Blend2D'; then github.com/LaurenzV/master-thesis main.pdf

name: Blend2D
baseline: Skia (CPU pipeline) and Cairo; also AGG, JUCE, Qt6, CoreGraphics
workload: Time for 1000 render calls of a single shape (rectangles, polygons, curves, strokes; solid/gradient/image paints) at sizes 8x8 to 256x256 on a 512x600 pixmap, single-threaded and 8-thread.
claimed_speedup: Third-party thesis: Blend2D is 'the clear winner', needing the shortest time 'for nearly all configurations' versus the C++ and Rust renderers. Fill-Solid-RectU 256x256 single-threaded: Blend2D 10.8 ms vs Skia 50.3 ms (about 4.7x faster, derived from page data) and Cairo 21.9 ms (about 2.0x faster, derived from page data) per 1000 renders. Blend2D 8-thread mode reaches 4.7x over its single-thread time on 256x256 in one test.
compiler_and_flags: not stated for the C++ renderers in the thesis
hardware: Apple M1 Pro (8 cores, 16 GB) for thesis figures; i9-14900K also run (vello_chart manifest.json)
tradeoffs: Optional JIT through AsmJit (a dependency only when JIT is enabled); C and C++ API; CPU-only; multi-threaded rendering context available.
caveats: Blend2D is itself one of the category's baselines; the entry records it as the strongest CPU rasterizer measured against Skia and Cairo. Numbers come from a third-party thesis whose benchmark harness is a fork of Blend2D's own (bl-samples / blend2d-apps); Skia and Cairo build flags and versions are not stated. blend2d.com performance page (the author's own charts) was not reachable.
found_via: Same thesis as the Vello CPU entry (WebSearch: 'sparse strips CPU GPU 2D vector graphics rendering Vello thesis benchmark Skia Blend2D')

name: Blaze (aurimasg/blaze)
workload: Multi-threaded CPU rasterization of large vector scenes (Paris-30k map, 4222x3474 px) and text, compared with Blend2D, Skia and CoreGraphics; each image rendered 500 times, 5 best and 5 worst dropped, remaining 490 averaged (per snippet of the author's article).
claimed_speedup: Search-result summaries of the author's article: Paris-30k (4222x3474, 50,681 layers) renders in 18 ms with Blaze vs 47 ms Blend2D, 190 ms Skia and 390 ms CoreGraphics (about 2.6x over Blend2D and about 10.6x over Skia, derived from snippet data); also described as around 20x faster than Core Graphics overall.  Snippet only.
hardware: Apple M1 Max, 10 cores (per search-result snippet of the author's article)
tradeoffs: Supports any POSIX-threads system (including WebAssembly) but not Windows; relies on fast bit counting and trailing-zero instructions; multi-threaded design, so single-thread wins are not claimed.
caveats: Snippet only: the numbers come from search-result summaries of the author's article gasiulis.name/parallel-rasterization-on-cpu (egress blocked, not opened), so thread counts, compiler and flags and whether Blend2D and Skia ran multi-threaded are unknown. Blaze itself is multi-threaded, so the win is partly parallelism rather than per-core speed. The repo carries Benchmarks/ code for Blaze, Blend2D, Skia and CoreGraphics (opened) but no results file. No Windows support. Capped at C.
found_via: WebSearch: '"vector graphics" rasterizer C++ "faster than Blend2D" OR "faster than Skia" CPU SIMD paper github 2025', then 'Gasiulis Parallel rasterization on CPU' and 'Blaze rasterizer Paris-30k M1 Max'; github.com/aurimasg/blaze opened

name: ThorVG
workload: CPU rendering of 5k semi-transparent primitives (shapes, strokes, images with bilinear filtering, alpha blending) at 2560x1440; geometry-heavy cases such as rectangles, strokes, rotation, circles.
claimed_speedup: README: an average of about 2.9x faster than 'a widely-used vector graphics engine' (the test conditions name Skia v148) in CPU benchmarks; advantage clearest in rectangles, strokes, rotations and circles.
hardware: Apple M2 Pro (macOS 26) per README test conditions
stars_or_usage: 1.9k stars; used by Canva, Godot, LVGL, Tizen
tradeoffs: Small footprint (about 170KB core); SVG Tiny and Lottie focus rather than full Skia feature set; CPU/SIMD, OpenGL, WebGPU backends.
caveats: First-party. Benchmark app is public (github.com/thorvg/thorvg.benchmark, MIT, compares ThorVG with Skia installed via vcpkg, 1000 measured frames plus 120 warmup) but compiler and flags are not stated, and the per-test chart is an image. The README does not name Skia in the headline claim; Skia v148 appears only in the test conditions. Skia ran on its default CPU path as set up through vcpkg (details not verified).
found_via: WebSearch: '"vector graphics" rasterizer C++ "faster than Blend2D" OR "faster than Skia" CPU SIMD paper github 2025' surfaced thorvg PR 4849; README and thorvg.benchmark opened

name: tiny-skia
workload: CPU 2D rendering of common operations (fills, strokes, gradients, patterns, clipping) in the project's benchmark set.
claimed_speedup: README: 20-100% slower than Skia on x86-64 and about 100-300% slower on ARM, 'which is still faster than cairo and raqote in many cases'.
tradeoffs: A minimal Skia subset ported to Rust (about 14k lines, about 200KB, no text, no GPU); not a Skia replacement. Needs FFI from C++.
caveats: The win over Cairo is stated only as 'in many cases' and the detailed results page (linebender.github.io/tiny-skia/x86_64.html) is blocked. It loses to Skia, so the claim is relative to Cairo only. In the Vello CPU thesis, tiny-skia is slower than Vello CPU and Skia in the shown tests, so the Cairo advantage may not hold across workloads (e.g. Fill-Solid-RectA 256x256: tiny-skia 136 ms vs Cairo 18.6 ms). Rust-only.
found_via: Read README after the Vello CPU thesis named tiny-skia as a compared Rust renderer

name: Rive Renderer (rive-runtime)
workload: Real-time GPU rendering of grids of animated vector tiles on an iPhone 12 Max (per search-result snippets of Rive's announcement and a LinkedIn post).
claimed_speedup: Snippet only: Skia rendered 9 tiles at about 100 ms (10 fps) while the Rive Renderer rendered 100 tiles at about 16 ms (60 fps); stated as '66x faster', 6000 tiles/sec vs 90 tiles/sec.
stars_or_usage: 1.2k stars; renderer used across Rive's Apple, Android, Flutter, Unity, Unreal and web runtimes
tradeoffs: GPU renderer with Metal, Vulkan, D3D11, D3D12 and OpenGL/WebGL backends, built on a geometric reduction of antialiased paths to triangle patches; part of the Rive runtime (state machines, .riv files), so adopting only the renderer needs extraction; the runtime repo also contains a Skia-based renderer for comparison.
caveats: Vendor claim by the company selling the product (retier to C), snippet only: the Rive blog post and the LinkedIn post are blocked or unopened. The rive-runtime README and renderer/README.md (both read) contain no benchmark numbers. Test scene is animation-heavy tile grids on a mobile GPU, not a general path-rendering benchmark; Skia configuration (Ganesh or Graphite, GPU or CPU) unstated.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Rive renderer C++ GPU vector rendering faster than Skia benchmark rive-runtime'; github.com/rive-app/rive-runtime opened

name: GPU scanline path rendering (Li, Hou, Zhou 2016)
baseline: state-of-the-art GPU path renderers (exact baselines not confirmed from an opened source)
workload: GPU path rendering of large vector scenes at Ultra HD resolution with high-quality anti-aliasing, parallelized over boundary fragments with non-boundary pixels filled as horizontal spans (SIGGRAPH Asia 2016, ACM TOG 35(6)).
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (ACM abstract as summarized by search): consistent 2.5x speedup over state-of-the-art alternatives for high-quality rendering at Ultra HD, more than 30x in extreme cases; 10x on animated input.
compiler_and_flags: Visual Studio 2013, CUDA 7.5 (per repo README; pre-built binary)
hardware: NVIDIA GPU with CUDA sm_50 and OpenGL 4.5; tested with NVIDIA driver 368.81 on 64-bit Windows 10 (per repo README)
tradeoffs: Windows plus NVIDIA only (CUDA, Thrust, Modern GPU segmented sort); research prototype with SDL, Boost and RapidXML dependencies; README warns gl_SampleMask behavior changed after driver 368.22.
caveats: Paper itself (dl.acm.org, kunzhou.net, researchgate) is blocked, so the compared systems, per-scene timings and GPU model were not seen; the numbers are from a search summary of the abstract. The named baselines in the paper are probably NV_path_rendering and MPVG but that is unconfirmed here, so baseline_in_list is false and the entry may not qualify under the named-baseline rule. The repo has no benchmark results; test data come from the MPVG project. Abandoned since 2017.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Efficient GPU path rendering using scanline rasterization Li Ma Wang source code github faster than NV_path_rendering Cairo'; github.com/Mochimazui/gpu-scanline-path-rendering opened

name: NV_path_rendering (NVpr)
language: C (OpenGL extension in the NVIDIA driver)
baseline: Cairo, Skia, Qt, Direct2D (nvpr_svg comparison in the NVprSDK)
workload: GPU stencil-then-cover path rendering of SVG-like scenes, compared in the NVprSDK nvpr_svg demo and the SIGGRAPH Asia 2012 paper 'GPU-accelerated Path Rendering' (Kilgard and Bolz).
claimed_speedup: Snippet only: search summaries say NVpr beats Qt, Skia and Cairo, and one summary quotes 8.69 ms at 1000x1000 with 16 samples against Cairo's 909 ms at 1000x1000 (attribution of that pair to this paper is not confirmed).
tradeoffs: Needs an NVIDIA GPU and driver exposing GL_NV_path_rendering; vendor-specific extension, not usable on AMD or Intel; the NVprSDK samples are NVIDIA-distributed, not an OSI-licensed repo that was opened here.
caveats: Paper-only entry for the research section. The paper PDF (developer.download.nvidia.com) and project pages were blocked, and no canonical code repository was opened (an unofficial demo repo, victusfate/nvpr_demo, appeared in search but was not opened). All numbers are from search-result snippets. Claim is old (2012 hardware) and the CPU baselines were of that era.
found_via: WebSearch: '2D vector path rasterization paper GPU faster than Skia Cairo' and 'github NV_path_rendering NVprSDK Kilgard sample code Skia Cairo Qt performance comparison'
